fixes.answer: I consider online privacy extremely important, though I admit I do not always protect it as well as I should. In an age where our data is constantly collected, I believe people have a fundamental right to control their personal information. The [[erosion]] of privacy can lead to manipulation and surveillance, which is genuinely worrying. So while convenience often tempts us to be careless, I think [[safeguarding]] our privacy is a vital and [[overlooked]] responsibility.

This is quite paradoxical. On one hand, awareness of privacy issues has grown enormously following major data scandals, so people claim to care more. On the other hand, our actual behaviour suggests otherwise; we [[readily]] hand over data for the sake of convenience and free services. This gap between concern and action is often called the [[privacy paradox]]. So people are more aware, yet often equally willing to [[compromise]] their privacy.
fixes.why: 'aware' and 'willing' are plain; marked 'readily' and 'privacy paradox'

fixes.answer: The consequences are significant and often hidden. Companies use our data to target advertising with [[uncanny]] precision, which can feel manipulative. More seriously, large data collections are vulnerable to breaches, potentially exposing people to fraud and identity theft. There is also the broader concern of this information being used to influence our behaviour and opinions. Essentially, it creates a huge [[imbalance]] of power that can [[undermine]] individual autonomy.

A society without privacy can become one of pervasive surveillance, which can have a [[chilling effect]] on free expression. If people feel constantly watched, they may [[self-censor]] and conform, which is unhealthy for democracy. The concentration of personal data in a few powerful hands also creates opportunities for manipulation on a mass scale. So the erosion of privacy is not merely a personal issue; it has profound [[implications]] for freedom itself.
fixes.why: 'freedom' is plain and repeated; marked 'chilling effect' and 'self-censor'

fixes.answer: I strongly disagree with that argument. Privacy is not about hiding wrongdoing; it is a fundamental right that protects our autonomy and dignity. We all have private thoughts and information that are simply [[nobody else's business]], regardless of innocence. This argument also dangerously assumes those in power will always act benevolently. In my view, defending privacy is about protecting freedom itself, not [[concealing]] anything [[sinister]].
fixes.why: 'freedom' is plain; marked the idiom 'nobody else's business'
